guide.summary: Gmail OAuth is easy to wire up but hard to ship. Almost every useful Gmail scope for an agent, such as gmail.readonly, gmail.modify and gmail.compose, is restricted. Restricted scopes need Google verification, which Google estimates at about 6 weeks without a guarantee. If your server stores or handles that data, you also need a paid third-party security assessment that you must repeat every 12 months. gmail.send is only sensitive and goes through a shorter review. Until you are verified, you are stuck in Testing mode, or you face a 100-user lifetime cap that can never be reset. Start on Composio's managed auth and only build your own app when you are ready to commit to verification.
auth_alternatives: Composio managed auth: choose it to ship now without running Google verification yourself. The trade-off is that users authorize Composio's OAuth client rather than yours.

Internal app (Google Workspace): choose it if every user is inside one Workspace organization you control. The trade-off is that only that organization can use it, and its administrator may need to approve it.
Testing publishing status: choose it for development or a small pilot with named test users. The trade-off is a tester warning screen, a user cap and refresh tokens with a limited lifetime.

Service accounts: choose them only for project-based data. Google positions them mainly for that rather than user-specific data, so they are not a substitute for per-user Gmail access in a consumer agent.

reasons_to_bring_own: Workspace administrators allow apps by OAuth client ID. With your own client, enterprise customers allowlist your app rather than a shared one.

If you will store or process restricted Gmail data on your own servers anyway, you face the security assessment yourself. Owning the verified app then lets you control the 12-month reassessment cycle.
build_or_borrow.verdict: Use Composio managed auth; you do not need your own app yet because Gmail's restricted scopes need roughly 6 weeks of verification plus a paid, annually repeated security assessment, and an unverified app of your own hits a permanent 100-user cap.

blockers.text: Gmail read and modify scopes are restricted and require restricted scope verification. Google estimates this at about 6 weeks and does not guarantee it.
blockers.workaround: Use Composio managed auth while you prepare. If you only need to send mail, ask for gmail.send alone, which is sensitive rather than restricted.

blockers.text: If restricted data touches your servers, you need a security assessment from a Google-empanelled assessor. You must repeat it at least every 12 months.
blockers.workaround: Budget for the assessor fee and calendar the renewal. Alternatively, rely on Composio's managed app.

blockers.text: Unverified apps with sensitive or restricted scopes get 100 new users over the project's lifetime. The cap cannot be reset, and when it runs out, Google sign-in can stop working.
blockers.workaround: Do not burn your production project's cap on casual testing. Use Testing mode with named test users until you are verified.

blockers.text: Google user data cannot be used to train or improve AI/ML models, including foundational models.
blockers.workaround: Keep Gmail data out of any training, fine-tuning or eval pipelines, and state this in your privacy policy.

blockers.text: If Google rejects the app, user access to the unapproved sensitive or restricted scopes stops working.
blockers.workaround: Request the minimum scopes you can justify and prepare clear scope justifications before you submit.

blockers.text: Workspace administrators can block authorization (admin_policy_enforced) until they allow your OAuth client ID.
blockers.workaround: Give enterprise customers your client ID and instructions for allowing it in Workspace admin controls.

app_specific_gotchas.text: The 100-user cap for unverified apps covers the whole life of the project and can never be reset. Burning it on testing permanently hurts that project.
Google returns a refresh token only when you set access_type=offline, and only on the first code exchange. If you miss it, you will not get one again on later exchanges.
The client secret is shown only once, at creation. You cannot view or download it again.
A compliant branding verification result is valid for only 7 days. If you do not publish branding in that window, you must verify again.
Publishing status defaults to Testing. Only listed test users can authorize, and their refresh tokens expire after a limited lifetime.

steps.title: Decide: build your own Google OAuth client or use Composio managed auth
steps.detail_md: Composio lists a `gmail` toolkit with managed auth available. Using it may save you from running your own client. The provided material does not say whose verified client that uses or how its limits apply to you, so confirm that with Composio before relying on it. The rest of this guide assumes you register your own client, which is the path that makes the integration fully yours.

steps.title: Pick the smallest scope set, knowing it decides your review path
steps.detail_md:
This choice sets how long you wait and what you pay, so make it before anything else.

- `gmail.send` is **sensitive**. It lets the app send email on the user's behalf.
- `gmail.readonly` is **restricted**. So are `gmail.modify`, `gmail.compose` and others.

Any sensitive or restricted scope requires verification unless an exception applies. Restricted scopes need restricted scope verification. If restricted data passes through or is stored on your servers, a paid third-party security assessment is also required, and it must be repeated yearly.

Google policy also forbids using Google user data to train or improve AI/ML models, including foundational models. For an AI agent, design around that from day one.

The agent can map each feature to the scope it needs. You make the call.

steps.title: Create a Google Cloud project and enable the Gmail API
steps.detail_md: Sign in to Google Cloud Console and create a project. Then open the API Library, select the Gmail API and click **Enable**. Do this before you create credentials.

steps.title: Choose Internal or External audience
steps.detail_md:
**Internal** apps are limited to your own Workspace organization and might need approval from an organization administrator. A public agent needs **External**.

The agent can explain the trade-off. You decide.

steps.title: Draft the privacy policy, consent-screen copy and redirect URI list
steps.detail_md:
The agent can draft the following:

- **Privacy policy.** It must be hosted on the same domain as your app home page. It should also state that Google user data is not used to train AI/ML models.
- **Redirect URIs.** Web server apps must list authorized redirect URIs on the client form. They must match exactly, including scheme, case and trailing slash. An `http://localhost` URI is fine for testing.

steps.title: Configure the consent screen and declare every scope on the Data Access page
steps.detail_md:
1. Fill in the branding fields.
2. Link the privacy policy on the OAuth consent screen.
3. Declare every scope you will request on the **Data Access** page. Google classifies each one there as sensitive or restricted.

steps.title: Create the OAuth web client and store the secret immediately
steps.detail_md:
Create a web application client and paste in the exact redirect URIs from step 5.

The client secret is shown **only once**, at creation. It cannot be viewed or downloaded again, so put it in your secret manager before you close the dialog.

steps.title: Add test users while the app is in Testing
steps.detail_md:
The Publishing Status defaults to **Testing**, which limits access to listed test users. Expect these limits while testing:

- Users see a tester warning screen.
- A user cap applies.
- Refresh tokens have a limited lifetime.

That is acceptable for development but not for real users.

steps.title: Write the OAuth integration code
steps.detail_md:
The agent can write the code with these details:

- **Authorization endpoint:** `https://accounts.google.com/o/oauth2/v2/auth` (HTTPS only).
- **Token endpoint:** `https://oauth2.googleapis.com/token`.
- **Refresh tokens:** set `access_type=offline`, or you get no refresh token. One is returned only on the first code exchange, so persist it.
- **No discovery:** mail.google.com serves no OIDC or OAuth discovery document (probes returned 404). Hardcode the endpoints above.

Service accounts are mainly for project data, not per-user mail, so they are not the right fit here.

steps.title: Test end to end on localhost with a test user
steps.detail_md:
Sign in as a listed test user through an `http://localhost` redirect. Confirm that:

- the code exchange works,
- a refresh token is returned, and
- API calls succeed.

Redirect mismatch errors usually come from scheme, case or trailing slash differences.

steps.title: Verify domain ownership in Google Search Console
steps.detail_md: Brand verification requires that you verify ownership of the project's authorized domains in Google Search Console. This usually involves DNS changes.

steps.title: Script the demo video
steps.detail_md: The agent can write a shot list for the demo video. It should show the OAuth grant flow and how each requested scope is used in the app.

steps.title: Record and upload the demo video as Unlisted on YouTube
steps.detail_md: Record the flow from the script and upload it to YouTube as **Unlisted**.

steps.title: Submit brand verification and publish branding
steps.detail_md:
Submit from the **Branding** page, then click **Publish branding**.

A compliant result is valid for only 7 days before re-verification is needed. Publish promptly once you get it.

steps.title: Wait for brand verification
steps.detail_md: Brand verification typically takes 2-3 business days. The estimate below uses about 3 calendar days.

steps.title: Submit scope verification
steps.detail_md:
Submit for sensitive or restricted scope verification.

Until you are verified, the app has a 100 new-user cap. The cap covers the project's whole lifetime and cannot be reset. Once it is exhausted, Google sign-in can be disabled, so do not burn it on wide beta testing.

If the app is rejected, user access to the unapproved scopes stops working.

steps.title: Wait for scope verification
steps.detail_md:
Expected review times:

- **Sensitive scopes:** 10 business days.
- **Restricted scopes:** about 6 weeks, not guaranteed.

The estimate below assumes restricted scopes. With only sensitive scopes, expect roughly two calendar weeks.

steps.title: Engage a Google-empanelled assessor (restricted scopes via your servers)
steps.detail_md:
This step applies if restricted-scope data is stored on, or passes through, your servers. You must then pass a security assessment by a Google-empanelled assessor.

Google charges no fee for the assessment. You and the assessor agree the cost between yourselves.

steps.title: Wait for the security assessment and Letter of Assessment
steps.detail_md: How long the assessment takes is **not documented** in the provided sources. The 0 below is a placeholder, not an estimate.

steps.title: Draft Workspace admin allowlisting instructions for customers
steps.detail_md:
A Google Workspace administrator can block a user's authorization (the `admin_policy_enforced` error) until they allow your OAuth client ID in Workspace admin controls.

The agent can write a short help page for customer admins that includes your client ID.

steps.title: Schedule annual reassessment
steps.detail_md: The security assessment and reverification must be repeated at least every 12 months after the Letter of Assessment approval date. Put a reminder in the calendar well before that date.

belief_diff.topic: Does letting arbitrary users connect require provider review or verification?
belief_diff.prior_belief: Yes, any Gmail OAuth app requested for arbitrary public users with sensitive or restricted Gmail scopes must pass Google OAuth app verification before general use.
belief_diff.finding: Claims say apps requesting sensitive or restricted scopes must complete verification unless they qualify for an exception, and Gmail restricted scopes require restricted scope verification.

belief_diff.prior_belief: Google OAuth verification typically takes about 3 to 5 business days, though restricted-scope reviews can run 4 to 6 weeks.
belief_diff.finding: Claims give brand verification at 2-3 business days, sensitive scope verification at 10 business days, and restricted scope verification at about 6 weeks (not guaranteed), so the 3-5 business day figure is not supported for sensitive-scope apps.

belief_diff.topic: Limits while the app is unapproved
belief_diff.prior_belief: An unverified app is capped at 100 users lifetime and shows an unverified-app warning screen to every user.
belief_diff.finding: Claims say unverified apps using sensitive or restricted scopes have a 100 new-user cap over the project's lifetime that cannot be reset, and Testing status shows a tester warning screen.

belief_diff.prior_belief: Google charges no fee for OAuth app verification, but restricted-scope apps may require a paid annual third-party security assessment such as a CASA review costing several thousand dollars.
belief_diff.finding: Claims say Google charges no fee for the security assessment and the cost is agreed between developer and assessor, and an annual assessment is required for restricted-scope apps accessing data via a third-party server; they do not give a dollar amount or name CASA.

belief_diff.topic: Key prerequisites (domain, privacy policy, video, business verification)
belief_diff.prior_belief: Yes, you need a verified owned domain, a publicly accessible privacy policy URL, a demo video showing scope usage, and a Google Cloud project with the consent screen configured; business verification is required for most apps.
belief_diff.finding: Claims support domain ownership verification in Search Console, a privacy policy on the app's domain linked from the consent screen, and an unlisted YouTube demo video; they do not address business verification or the requirement for a consent screen as stated.

belief_diff.prior_belief: Redirect URIs must be registered exactly in the Cloud Console, must use HTTPS except for localhost, and cannot contain wildcards or fragments.
belief_diff.finding: Claims say redirect URIs must match exactly including scheme, case and trailing slash, and http://localhost is allowed for testing; they do not state the HTTPS rule, wildcard ban, or fragment ban explicitly.
